whyNext: Builds on hash set duplicate detection from Contains Duplicate (Seq 1) by enforcing a sliding window distance constraint of at most k indices.
hints: Consider how tracking element indices or maintaining a bounded window can verify the distance constraint.
Use a sliding window HashSet of maximum size k or a HashMap storing the most recent index of each value.
As you iterate through the array, check if the current element exists in your window of size k; if present, return true, otherwise insert it and remove the element that fell outside the window.

brute.idea: Compare each element with every other element within the next k positions using nested loops.
steps: Iterate i from 0 to n - 1.
Iterate j from i + 1 up to min(i + k, n - 1).
If nums[i] equals nums[j], return true.
If no such pair is found after scanning all elements, return false.
brute.whySlow: Scanning k elements for every index takes O(n * k) time in the worst case.

optimal.idea: Maintain a sliding window HashSet containing at most k elements to detect duplicates in constant time.
steps: Initialize an empty HashSet to hold elements within the current window.
Iterate through nums with index i.
If the set already contains nums[i], return true.
Add nums[i] to the set.
If the set size exceeds k, remove nums[i - k] to maintain the window size.
Return false if the iteration finishes without finding any duplicate.

whyNext: Extends set-based existence lookups from Contains Duplicate II (Seq 301) to two distinct collections by retaining only values present in both sets.
hints: Think about converting one array to a set for quick existence tests, while collecting unique matches.
Use two HashSets: one for the first array and one to collect unique intersection elements from the second array.
Populate a set with elements of nums1, then iterate through nums2 and add elements that exist in the first set to an intersection set, then convert it to an array.

brute.idea: Iterate over nums1 and for each unique element search linearly through nums2.
steps: Create a list or set to store common unique elements.
For each element in nums1, search through all elements of nums2.
If found and not already in result list, add it.
Convert the result list to an array.
brute.whySlow: Searching nums2 for every element in nums1 takes O(n * m) time.

optimal.idea: Store nums1 elements in a HashSet and filter nums2 against the set to collect unique common items.
steps: Insert all elements of nums1 into set1.
Create an empty set for the result.
Iterate through nums2; if an element is in set1, add it to the result set.
Convert the result set into an integer array.

whyNext: Transitions from unique set intersection in Seq 302 to multiset intersection by tracking element frequencies across both collections.
hints: Each element must appear in the result as many times as it shows in both arrays.
Use a frequency HashMap for one array and decrement counts as you encounter matching elements in the second array.
Count occurrences of each number in nums1 with a map; scan nums2, and whenever an item has count > 0 in the map, append it to the result and decrement its count.

brute.idea: Mark matched elements in a boolean array for nums2 to handle duplicate frequencies without hash maps.
steps: Create a boolean array visited for nums2 initialized to false.
For each element in nums1, find the first unvisited match in nums2.
Mark that index in visited as true and record the element.
Convert the gathered elements into an array.
brute.whySlow: Linear search across nums2 for each element in nums1 takes O(n * m) time.

optimal.idea: Count occurrences of elements in nums1 using a HashMap, then decrement counts when scanning nums2.
steps: Populate a frequency HashMap with elements of nums1.
Initialize an output list for matched numbers.
Iterate through nums2; if the current number exists in the map with count > 0, append it to the list and decrement the count in the map.
Convert the result list to an array and return it.

whyNext: Builds on frequency map construction from Intersection of Two Arrays II (Seq 303) by validating that all value occurrence counts are pairwise distinct.
hints: Count each value's occurrences first, then check if any two values share the same frequency.
Use a HashMap to record frequencies and a HashSet to verify that the set of frequency values contains no duplicates.
Iterate through the array to populate the frequency map, then insert each frequency count into a HashSet. If the size of the set equals the number of keys in the map, all counts are unique.

brute.idea: Calculate the frequency of each distinct element, collect them in a list, and compare all pairs for equality.
steps: Collect distinct elements from arr.
Count occurrences of each distinct element by scanning arr.
Compare each count with every other count using nested loops.
Return false if any two counts match, otherwise true.
brute.whySlow: Counting elements repeatedly takes O(n * u) where u is distinct values, plus pairwise frequency comparison.

optimal.idea: Count frequencies using a map, then insert all counts into a set to verify uniqueness.
steps: Populate a frequency HashMap from arr.
Insert all values of the map into a HashSet.
Check if the size of the set matches the number of keys in the map.
Return true if sizes match, otherwise false.

whyNext: Builds on missing value identification from Missing Number (Seq 13) by detecting multiple absent values in [1, n] using sign-inversion index marking.
hints: Can you use the array indices themselves as hash buckets without allocating additional memory?
Mark visits by inverting the sign of the element at index abs(val) - 1.
Iterate through nums; for each value, find idx = abs(val) - 1 and negate nums[idx] if positive. On a second pass, any index with a positive value corresponds to a missing number idx + 1.

brute.idea: Store all numbers in a HashSet, then check every integer from 1 to n to see which ones are missing.
steps: Insert all elements of nums into a HashSet.
Loop integer i from 1 to nums.length.
If i is not present in the set, append i to the result list.
Return the result list.
brute.whySlow: Allocates O(n) auxiliary space for the HashSet instead of reusing existing storage.

optimal.idea: Use the array indices as implicit hash buckets by negating values at index abs(x) - 1 to achieve O(1) extra space.
steps: Iterate through nums. For each element x, let targetIdx = abs(x) - 1.
If nums[targetIdx] is positive, negate it to mark that (targetIdx + 1) has been seen.
Perform a second pass: for any index i where nums[i] > 0, add (i + 1) to the missing numbers list.
Return the collected list of missing numbers.

whyNext: Extends sign-inversion index marking from Find All Numbers Disappeared (Seq 305) to simultaneously isolate both the duplicated value and the missing number in [1, n].
hints: When indexing abs(x) - 1, encountering an already negative value reveals the duplicate, while a positive slot at the end reveals the missing number.
Use sign negation to identify the duplicate during iteration, then identify the missing number by finding the positive index.
Traverse nums; for each x, let idx = abs(x) - 1. If nums[idx] < 0, x is the duplicate. Otherwise negate nums[idx]. In a second pass, the index i where nums[i] > 0 gives missing = i + 1.

brute.idea: Count the frequency of each number from 1 to n using an auxiliary frequency array.
steps: Allocate a frequency array counts of size n + 1.
Iterate through nums and increment counts[x] for each element.
Scan from 1 to n: find which number has count == 2 (duplicate) and which has count == 0 (missing).
Return [duplicate, missing].
brute.whySlow: Requires an extra array of size n + 1 for counting.

optimal.idea: Mark indices negative to detect the duplicate on the first pass, then identify the remaining positive index for the missing number.
steps: Initialize dup and missing to -1.
For each value x in nums, inspect nums[abs(x) - 1]. If it is already negative, abs(x) is the duplicate; otherwise negate it.
Scan nums again: if nums[i] is positive, missing is i + 1.
Return [dup, missing].

whyNext: Builds on single-pass array traversal from Set Mismatch (Seq 306) by maintaining a running tally of consecutive ones that resets upon encountering zero.
hints: Keep track of the current streak of ones and update the maximum streak seen so far.
Iterate once through the binary array, incrementing a streak counter on 1 and resetting to 0 on 0.
Initialize count and maxCount to 0. For each number, if it is 1, increment count and update maxCount; if 0, reset count to 0. Return maxCount.

brute.idea: For every index i with value 1, scan forward to count the length of consecutive ones.
steps: Initialize maxConsecutive = 0.
For each index i, if nums[i] == 1, iterate j from i forward while nums[j] == 1.
Update maxConsecutive = max(maxConsecutive, j - i).
Return maxConsecutive.
brute.whySlow: Redundant forward scans can take O(n²) time in the worst case when array is all 1s.

optimal.idea: One-pass linear scan keeping a running count of ones and resetting on zeros.
steps: Initialize currentCount = 0 and maxCount = 0.
Iterate through each number in nums.
If the number is 1, increment currentCount and set maxCount = max(maxCount, currentCount).
If the number is 0, reset currentCount = 0.
Return maxCount.

whyNext: Builds on local condition checking from Max Consecutive Ones (Seq 307) by detecting an inversion in monotonicity and determining if a single element modification can resolve it.
hints: Count how many times nums[i] > nums[i + 1]. If it happens more than once, it is impossible.
When an inversion occurs, decide whether to lower nums[i] or raise nums[i + 1] based on nums[i - 1].
If nums[i] > nums[i+1], increment count. If count > 1, return false. Check if i == 0 or nums[i-1] <= nums[i+1]; if so, conceptually lower nums[i]. Otherwise raise nums[i+1] = nums[i].

brute.idea: Try modifying each element one by one to see if the resulting array becomes non-decreasing.
steps: First check if the original array is already non-decreasing.
For each index i from 0 to n - 1, save original value nums[i].
Try setting nums[i] = nums[i-1] (or nums[i+1] if i == 0) and check if sorted.
If any modification yields a non-decreasing array, return true; otherwise return false.
brute.whySlow: Testing n possible modifications each taking O(n) check time yields O(n²) total time.

optimal.idea: Greedily resolve inversions in a single pass; allow at most one violation by adapting either nums[i] or nums[i+1].
steps: Initialize a violation counter modified = 0.
Iterate i from 0 to nums.length - 2.
If nums[i] > nums[i + 1]: increment modified; if modified > 1 return false.
If i == 0 or nums[i - 1] <= nums[i + 1], lower nums[i] = nums[i + 1]; otherwise raise nums[i + 1] = nums[i].
Return true if loop completes.

whyNext: Expands single-violation boundary detection from Non-decreasing Array (Seq 308) into finding the full bounded span of unsorted elements using prefix max and suffix min scans.
hints: Any element in the unsorted subarray must be placed such that elements to its left are smaller and elements to its right are larger.
Identify the rightmost element smaller than the running maximum and the leftmost element larger than the running minimum.

Scan left-to-right maintaining the running max; whenever nums[i] < runningMax, mark right boundary at i. Scan right-to-left maintaining running min; whenever nums[i] > runningMin, mark left boundary at i. Result is right - left + 1.

brute.idea: Compare the original array against a fully sorted clone to identify the first and last mismatching positions.
steps: Create a sorted copy of nums.
Find the first index l from the left where nums[l] != sorted[l].
Find the first index r from the right where nums[r] != sorted[r].
If no mismatches exist, return 0; otherwise return r - l + 1.
brute.whySlow: Sorting an array copy requires O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

optimal.idea: Find boundaries in a single two-way pass by tracking the running max from left and running min from right.
steps: Initialize end = -1, start = -1, max = -infinity, min = +infinity.
Iterate i from 0 to n - 1: update max = max(max, nums[i]). If nums[i] < max, set end = i.
Simultaneously iterate from right (n - 1 - i): update min = min(min, nums[n - 1 - i]). If nums[n - 1 - i] > min, set start = n - 1 - i.
If end == -1, array is already sorted, return 0; else return end - start + 1.

whyNext: Builds on running cumulative state from Product of Array Except Self (Seq 9) by computing the foundational 1D prefix sum array where each index stores the sum of all preceding elements.
hints: Each position in the running sum is simply the previous running sum plus the current element.
Use prefix accumulation to compute each element in-place or into a new array.
Iterate from index 1 to n - 1 and set nums[i] += nums[i - 1], then return nums.

brute.idea: For every index i, sum all elements from 0 to i using an inner loop.
steps: Allocate a new result array of size n.
For each index i, initialize sum = 0.
Loop j from 0 to i and add nums[j] to sum.
Assign res[i] = sum.
Return res.
brute.whySlow: Summing from 0 to i for every position takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Compute the cumulative sum in a single linear pass by accumulating into the array in-place.
steps: Iterate i from 1 to nums.length - 1.
Update nums[i] = nums[i] + nums[i - 1].
Return the modified nums array.

whyNext: Applies the prefix sum array created in Running Sum of 1d Array (Seq 310) to answer arbitrary range sum queries in constant O(1) time.
hints: Instead of summing between left and right on every query, precompute prefix sums during initialization.
Prefix sum array with prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i] enables sumRange(L, R) = prefix[R + 1] - prefix[L].
Construct a prefix array of size n + 1. In sumRange(left, right), directly return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left].

brute.idea: Store the raw array and iterate from left to right on every sum query.
steps: Store a copy of nums in the constructor.
In sumRange(left, right), loop from left to right and sum all values.
Return the computed sum.
brute.whySlow: Each range query takes O(n) time, leading to O(q * n) time for q queries.

optimal.idea: Precompute an (n+1)-sized prefix sum array to answer any range sum query in O(1) time via subtraction.
steps: Allocate prefix array of size n + 1 with prefix[0] = 0.
Fill prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i] for all i from 0 to n - 1.
In sumRange(left, right), return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left].

whyNext: Generalizes 1D prefix sum subtraction from Range Sum Query (Seq 311) to 2D matrices using 2D inclusion-exclusion principle for O(1) rectangular sum queries.
hints: Can you calculate the sum of any rectangle using submatrices starting from (0,0)?
Use 2D prefix sums where prefix[r][c] represents the sum of the submatrix from (0,0) to (r-1,c-1).
Fill prefix[r+1][c+1] = matrix[r][c] + prefix[r][c+1] + prefix[r+1][c] - prefix[r][c]. Query result is prefix[r2+1][c2+1] - prefix[r1][c2+1] - prefix[r2+1][c1] + prefix[r1][c1].

brute.idea: Iterate across the designated rows and columns for each query to sum all cells.
steps: Store the matrix in constructor.
In sumRegion(r1, c1, r2, c2), use nested loops from r1 to r2 and c1 to c2.
Accumulate and return the sum.
brute.whySlow: Summing cell by cell takes O(m * n) time per query.

optimal.idea: Precompute 2D prefix sums to evaluate any rectangular region in O(1) time using inclusion-exclusion.
steps: Initialize prefix matrix dp of size (m + 1) x (n + 1).
Fill dp[r + 1][c + 1] = matrix[r][c] + dp[r][c + 1] + dp[r + 1][c] - dp[r][c].
To query (r1, c1, r2, c2), return dp[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] - dp[r1][c2 + 1] - dp[r2 + 1][c1] + dp[r1][c1].
optimal.time: O(1) per query, O(m * n) setup

whyNext: Builds on running prefix sums from Running Sum of 1d Array (Seq 310) by comparing running left sum with total sum minus current element to find an equilibrium pivot index.
hints: The sum of numbers strictly to the left must equal totalSum - leftSum - nums[i].
First compute the total array sum; then maintain a running leftSum as you iterate from left to right.
Iterate through nums; if leftSum == totalSum - leftSum - nums[i], return current index. Otherwise add nums[i] to leftSum. Return -1 if not found.

brute.idea: For every index i, sum elements from 0 to i-1 and elements from i+1 to n-1 and check equality.
steps: Iterate i from 0 to n - 1.
Calculate leftSum by adding nums[0..i-1].
Calculate rightSum by adding nums[i+1..n-1].
If leftSum == rightSum, return i.
Return -1 if no pivot matches.
brute.whySlow: Summing left and right partitions for each index takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Precalculate total sum, then iterate while maintaining running left sum to check equality in O(1) per index.
steps: Calculate totalSum by summing all elements in nums.
Initialize leftSum = 0.
For each index i and value nums[i]: check if leftSum == totalSum - leftSum - nums[i]; if so return i.
Add nums[i] to leftSum.
Return -1 if no pivot index satisfies the condition.

whyNext: Builds on prefix remainder hashing from Subarray Sum Equals K (Seq 11) by storing prefix sum modulo k in a hash map to detect divisible subarray spans of length at least two.
hints: If prefixSum[j] % k == prefixSum[i] % k and j - i >= 2, the subarray between i and j has a sum that is a multiple of k.
Track the earliest index where each remainder (prefixSum % k) was encountered using a HashMap.

Initialize map with {0: -1}. Maintain running sum modulo k. If the remainder exists in map, check if (currentIdx - map[remainder] >= 2). If so return true; otherwise record map[remainder] = currentIdx.

brute.idea: Check all subarray spans of length >= 2 and test if their sum is a multiple of k.
steps: Iterate i from 0 to n - 2.
Initialize sum = nums[i].
Iterate j from i + 1 to n - 1.
Add nums[j] to sum. If sum % k == 0, return true.
Return false if no matching subarray is found.
brute.whySlow: Checking all pairs of endpoints takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Store the earliest index of each prefix remainder modulo k in a HashMap to verify a distance >= 2 in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize HashMap remainderMap with (0 -> -1) to handle subarrays starting from index 0.
Maintain running sum = 0.
For each index i, add nums[i] to sum and compute remainder = sum % k.
If remainder exists in map: if i - map.get(remainder) >= 2, return true.
Else: store map.put(remainder, i).
Return false if iteration ends without finding such a subarray.
